performers: Musopen Symphony (Commons credit; ensemble attribution disputed)
intro: A quiet string arpeggio shoots upwards and the orchestra answers fiercely. Even the finale’s lyrical second tune eventually comes back in G minor; Mozart holds to that key right to the end.

cues.title: Upwards, then the answer
cues.text: The strings climb quietly through a G minor chord. The orchestra answers with a forceful rush. Mozart keeps setting the two against each other: the spare rising phrase and the crowded reply.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 1–16. The triadic opening and rushing violin response are described by Marianne Williams Tobias: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Violins and winds soften
cues.text: The second theme sings in B♭ major, shared by violins and winds. Its longer notes make a welcome space in this fast movement. The accompanying pulse continues underneath.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, second group, pp. 37–38 of the numbered scan; Tobias’s Indianapolis Symphony note describes the violin-and-wind melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Shockingly voluptuous”
cues.text: The pianist and critic Charles Rosen finds pleasure inside Mozart’s pain: “In all of Mozart’s supreme expressions of suffering and terror … there is something shockingly voluptuous.”
cues.evidence: Charles Rosen, as quoted in Michael Steinberg, The Symphony: A Listener’s Guide (Oxford, 1995), and in Marianne Williams Tobias’s Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra programme note: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/. In the original sentence the dash list continues through the G minor Symphony, Don Giovanni and Pamina’s aria; Rosen’s own book was not opened.

cues.title: The leap breaks loose
cues.text: At the development, the opening leap returns in a jagged unison, studded with chromatic notes. The strings then chase fragments of it through overlapping entries. The tidy arpeggio has become difficult to pin down.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 125–170: chromatic opening of the development and subsequent imitative writing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horns without trumpets
cues.text: The whole symphony uses horns, woodwinds and strings. Mozart leaves out trumpets and timpani. Even the finale’s fiercest answers come from this comparatively small orchestra.
cues.evidence: Instrumentation in both versions of K. 550, listed at https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.40_in_G_minor,_K.550_(Mozart,_Wolfgang_Amadeus).

cues.title: The first leap again
cues.text: The quiet rising figure is back in G minor, with its fierce answer still attached. After the development’s chromatic scrambling, the notes of the opening chord are suddenly clear again.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, recapitulation from bar 206.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tune turns minor
cues.text: The gentle second theme returns in G minor. Its familiar curves remain, but the earlier B♭ major warmth has gone. The symphony keeps this minor key through its final chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, recapitulated second group and final cadence, pp. 46–49 of the numbered scan.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The most discussed symphony
cues.text: Neal Zaslaw says of K. 550: “No symphony of Mozart’s, not even the ‘Jupiter’, has aroused so much comment as this one.” Otto Jahn, in the nineteenth century, hears in it “sorrow and complaining”, and in the finale “a wild merriment that seeks to drown sorrow”.
cues.evidence: Neal Zaslaw, Mozart’s Symphonies: Context, Performance Practice, Reception (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1989): the sentence appears in the book (Internet Archive full-text excerpt, page not seen) and is quoted in Marianne Williams Tobias’s note: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/. Otto Jahn, Life of Mozart, trans. P. D. Townsend (1882), vol. 3, chapter on instrumental music: “Sorrow and complaining take the place of joy and gladness”; the finale “brings no peace, only a wild merriment that seeks to drown sorrow”: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/43413

transitions.title: F prepares the gentler tune
transitions.from: A · Rising strings, fierce orchestral answer
transitions.to: B · A gentler tune in B♭
transitions.how: The transition gathers on F, the dominant of B♭ major. After the break, violins and woodwinds share the quieter second theme. Longer notes replace the opening’s rushing answer, while the Allegro assai pulse continues.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, transition and second-group opening, pp. 36–37 of the numbered scan.

transitions.title: A jagged answer to B♭
transitions.from: B · A gentler tune in B♭
transitions.how: The exposition closes in B♭ major. Its successor is the opening leap stretched into a chromatic unison: the orchestra briefly loses the comfort of a supporting chord. The strings then take up fragments in imitation, one entry pursuing another.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 118–140.

transitions.title: D leads back to G
transitions.to: A′ · The G minor leap returns
transitions.how: The running string fragments lead to D, the dominant of G minor. The opening arpeggio returns quietly in the strings over its original G minor harmony. Then comes the familiar forceful answer.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 193–214.

transitions.title: D prepares the changed melody
transitions.from: A′ · The G minor leap returns
transitions.to: B′ · The gentle tune in G minor
transitions.how: The returning transition prepares G minor through its dominant, D. Violins and winds resume the quieter second theme in that home key. The orchestral contrast survives; the earlier change to B♭ major is replaced by a G minor melody.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, recapitulatory transition and second group, pp. 45–47 of the numbered scan.

source.title: Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke VIII/40 (1880), plate W.A.M. 550; parts common to both versions
source.locator: IV. Allegro assai, PDF pp. 33–49: opening arpeggio, second theme, development and recapitulation. The edition prints both orchestral versions.

timeline.note: The violins’ quiet rising arpeggio is supported by bassoons and lower strings.
Winds and horns reinforce the running string figures.
The violins’ gentler B♭ major tune alternates with wind replies.
The opening arpeggio breaks into a chromatic unison, then passes between imitating parts.
The quiet rising arpeggio returns in the violins, with bassoons and lower strings.
The gentler second theme returns in G minor, with strings and winds answering each other.
Running strings press towards the close beneath held and accented wind chords.

quote.source: Mozart to his father Leopold, Vienna, 13 October 1781; our translation

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
